catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomeu-l:
Bartholomeu Lourenço de Gusmão was a naturalist and the first aeronaut, born at Santos, Brazil, in 1685, who died at Toledo in 1724. He left a Jesuit novitiate at Bahia in 1701, studied at Coimbra, and became Doctor of Canon Law. In 1709 he petitioned John V of Portugal for privilege over his airship invention, with great confidence. His design spread a huge sail over a bark, with bellows blowing air through tubes when wind failed.

Magnets in hollow metal balls were to propel it, though gases and hot air likely filled the shells instead. The public test set for 24 June 1709 never took place, but he made lesser experiments descending from heights. His contrivance embodied the kite's principle, and he also wrote on navigating the air and pumping leaking ships. Charged before the Inquisition on another matter, he fled to Spain and died of fever at Toledo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curacao:
A mission entry covers Curacao, a vicariate apostolic embracing the Dutch West Indies: Curacao, Bonaire, and Aruba, plus Saba, St. Eustatius, and Dutch St. Martin. Discovered by Ojeda in 1499, the islands first heard Spanish Hieronymite missionaries from Santo Domingo. Spain held Curacao until 1634, when the Dutch West India Company banned Catholic practice under severe penalties.

Jesuits still worked in secret from 1701 to 1742. A first prefect apostolic came in 1772, Dutch Franciscans followed in 1776, and M. J. Nieuwindt, appointed prefect in 1824, became first vicar apostolic when the vicariate was erected in 1842. Dutch Dominicans took charge in 1868. Nine-tenths of the people were Catholics, served by churches, schools, hospitals, and two Catholic newspapers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-damao:
A diocesan entry describes Damao, a suffragan see of Goa in Portuguese India and the Bombay presidency, erected by Leo XIII in 1886 under a concordat settling Goa's claims against Propaganda. Dom Antonio Pedro da Costa, nominated by Portugal's king, took possession in June 1887, and the church of Bom Jesus became his cathedral.

The city, on the Arabian Sea about 100 miles north of Bombay, first met the Portuguese in 1523 when a storm drove Diogo de Mello into its harbour. Sacked in 1529, it heard its first Mass in 1541 and was finally secured in 1558 when its larger native garrison fled before 3,000 attackers. The diocese also held churches in Bombay itself, including Nossa Senhora da Gloria in Mazagon, the bishop's Bombay residence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernando-cast:
Fernando Castro Palao was a Spanish Jesuit moral theologian famed for holy life and learning. Born at Leon in 1581, he entered the Jesuits in 1596. He taught at Valladolid, Compostella, and Salamanca: philosophy, moral theology, and theology in turn. He became rector at Medina and consultor of the Inquisition.

Students flocked in great numbers to his moral theology classes at Compostella. His decisions were treated as oracles on the hardest cases sent to him. His Opus Morale spans seven volumes on all moral theology. Alphonsus and Gury rank him among the chief guides on moral theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-macao: A 1913 entry on Macao — the Chinese diocese. João Paulino d'Azevedo e Castro gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the Pearl River flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the far eastern port. Its 1576 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mattheus-pinn: This 1913 reference article on Encarnacão — a Portuguese writer of note. Michael Ott lists his works. Little is known of his career. The seventeenth century was his period. The learned press knew his pen. His 1690 works are famed. His 1690 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pharao: Pharao is the Exodus king whose hardened heart brought the plagues upon Egypt. This entry examines his identity, his role in the sacred history, and the traditions about him. The tyrant who defied Moses: his name echoes through every Passover.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preto-ribeira: Ribeirão Preto, the São Paulo city of the coffee lands, became a diocese. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history as of 1913. The faith in Brazil's coffee country: its new cathedral serves the wealthy coffee planters of São Paulo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sao-luiz-de-m: São Luiz de Maranhão became the archdiocese of Brazil's north coast. This entry covers its archbishops, its cathedral, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Maranhão isle: its old cathedral crowns São Luiz in Brazil's north in the state.
podcast-dannyjones-qr1PFNRgOao:
Physicist David Chester joins Danny Jones to talk about UFO physics and a secret race toward anti-gravity. Chester works on the math of how such craft might fly. His talk stays close to fields, mass, and energy.

Chester lays out how anti-gravity might work if the reports of craft are true. He names the labs and states he thinks are in the race. Jones asks what a win in that race would mean for war and travel. Listeners with a taste for hard science get a dense talk. The library files it as an archive record.
podcast-dannyjones-wTNBhMZz2Ao:
Analyst Scott Horton joins Danny Jones to warn that the Pentagon is on red alert and Mossad has been named the top threat. The episode title quotes Horton's alarm. Horton is a writer and radio host known for anti-war work.

Horton lays out the clash he sees between US and Israeli spy aims. He argues the bond hides a deep spy war that now nears a break. Jones asks what proof backs the red alert claim. Listeners get a tense brief on a bond most press treats as iron. The library files the talk as an archive record of his stated view.
podcast-joerogan-ONV76ZfcPao:
Comedian Duncan Trussell joins Joe Rogan for episode 2247 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Trussell is a comic and mystic whose talks with Rogan are famed for their wild, warm roam. He hosts a show of his own with the same loose soul.

Trussell and Rogan drift from death and God to drugs, love, and the end of the world, laughing all the way. The talk has no map, and that is the charm his fans seek. Rogan plays the straight man to Trussell's cosmic riffs. Listeners get a long, strange hug of a talk. The library keeps the episode as a record of their bond.
podcast-joerogan-Rxmw9eizOAo:
Graham Hancock joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1284 to argue for a lost civilization. Hancock's books claim that an advanced culture fell at the end of the ice age and passed its knowledge to the ancient world. By this visit, the case was already a show staple.

He updates Rogan on the sites and finds he rates highest, from carved stone in Turkey to flood tales on every continent. Rogan asks how the experts answer, and Hancock gives his view of their blindness. The episode is a mid-arc statement of the theory that later reached a mass TV audience.
